title: React Forms, Validation, and Accessible Errors
description: Build usable forms in React, distinguish controlled and uncontrolled inputs, validate data without losing accessibility, and understand when a form library is useful.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish controlled inputs from uncontrolled inputs and choose intentionally.
Use form submit handlers and prevent the browser's default navigation when handling submission in React.
Validate required fields, formats, and cross-field conditions while keeping validation separate from server authorization.
Render accessible error messages associated with the correct fields.
Explain what a form library such as React Hook Form manages and what it does not replace.
Build a registration form that handles input, validation, success, and server-error states.
Choose when to validate a field (onChange, onBlur, or onSubmit).
Use one typed object and a name-based handler for a multi-field form.
Use React Hook Form registration, submission, errors and pending state while understanding its limits.
Implement and retest cross-field validation without leaving stale accessible errors.

blocks.text: A form is a data-entry contract

A form collects values, communicates what is required, validates them, and submits a deliberate payload. In React, decide which values need to be state, which can be read from native form controls, and when validation should run. Good form behavior includes keyboard support, meaningful labels, clear error messages, preservation of entered data after a correctable error, and explicit loading/success/failure feedback.
Controlled and uncontrolled inputs

A controlled input receives its displayed value from React state and updates that state in onChange. This gives the component direct access to the current value and makes conditional behavior easier, but it requires careful updates and can add state work for every keystroke. An uncontrolled input keeps its current value in the DOM; React can read it at submission through FormData or a ref. Both patterns are valid—choose based on the form's needs, not a blanket rule.

blocks.text: One state object for a multi-field form

A single typed object makes the form payload easier to inspect and submit. Give each input a name matching its property and use one handler to update that property. Spread the previous object first, otherwise the other values can be lost.

steps.title: Keep fields in one typed object
steps.explanation: The object describes the payload; every field reads from one source of truth.

steps.title: Use name to identify the edited field
steps.explanation: The name attribute links an input to a property; the actual name must match an object key.

steps.title: Spread the previous object before updating one field
steps.explanation: Without spread, updating one field could discard other values.

steps.title: Connect every field to the shared state
steps.explanation: Each input uses value/onChange, and its name matches an object property.

blocks.text: Validation has layers

Native HTML constraints such as required, type=email, minLength, and pattern can catch common mistakes early and provide basic browser feedback. Application validation handles rules specific to the product, such as matching password fields or disallowed combinations. The server must validate again because client-side checks can be bypassed. Validation improves data quality and user experience; it is not an authorization or security boundary.

steps.title: Model field-specific errors
steps.explanation: The errors object can contain a message for each field but does not require a message for every field. This shape helps render an error next to the input that caused it.

steps.title: Validate each rule deliberately
steps.explanation: Each condition represents one product rule. These checks are only illustrative; production password and email policies should match documented product requirements.

steps.title: Return the validation result
steps.explanation: The caller can decide whether to display errors or proceed. A validator should report the result rather than unexpectedly modifying unrelated UI state.

blocks.text: Use the browser's built-in constraints deliberately

required demands a value, type="email" checks an email-shaped value, minLength sets a minimum text length, and pattern checks a regular expression. These constraints give early feedback but do not cover every product rule, prove an email exists, or replace server validation.

blocks.caption: Native HTML constraints in JSX
blocks.code:
<label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" required autoComplete="email" />
<label htmlFor="password">Password</label>
<input id="password" name="password" type="password" required minLength={8} />
<label htmlFor="phone">Phone number</label>
<input id="phone" name="phone" type="tel" pattern="[0-9]{7,15}" title="Enter 7–15 digits."/>

blocks.text: Choose when validation should run

Validation timing affects UX. Give the user time to finish entering a value, while still showing feedback soon enough to correct it. A common approach is onBlur first, then revalidation after edits; a short form may validate on submit, while a password-strength meter can react immediately.

items: onChange — validate after each edit. Useful for a password-strength meter, but may show premature errors.
onBlur — validate when the field loses focus, including keyboard Tab navigation. Often a good starting point for field errors.
onSubmit — validate on submission. Simple for short forms, but feedback arrives later.
After first interaction, revalidate as fields change if helpful. Avoid showing every required-field error on initial render.

blocks.text: Validate relationships between fields

Some rules depend on more than one value, such as confirming a password or requiring an end date after a start date. Keep these rules in a validation function that receives the current form values and returns field-specific errors. Re-run dependent checks when either related value changes; clear or replace stale errors. A client-side match check is feedback only—the server must still enforce its own account and business rules.

blocks.prompt: A user changes `password` after `confirmPassword` was previously valid. What should a form do next?

options.text: Revalidate the relationship and update or clear the confirmation error
options.feedback: The validity of confirmation depends on both current values, so changing either value can make the previous result stale.

options.text: Keep the previous result because confirmPassword itself did not change
options.feedback: The rule depends on two fields, so the unchanged confirmation value can become invalid when the password changes.

options.text: Treat a client-side match as proof the server can trust the submitted account data
options.feedback: Client checks can be bypassed and do not establish authorization or server-side validity.

options.text: Remove the error text and keep aria-invalid true permanently
options.feedback: Error state and its accessible description should reflect current validation results, not remain stale.

blocks.explanation: Cross-field validation depends on the current values of every related field. Update both the visible error and its accessible relationship, and repeat security-sensitive validation on the server.

blocks.text: Make errors accessible and actionable

Every field needs a programmatic label. When a field is invalid, display a specific message close to the field, associate it using aria-describedby, and set aria-invalid when appropriate. After submission, consider moving focus to an error summary or the first invalid field. Do not communicate errors by color alone, and avoid messages such as “Invalid input” when the learner needs to know how to fix the value.

blocks.text: When a form library helps

A library such as React Hook Form can manage field registration, validation state, submission, and performance-sensitive subscriptions with less custom wiring. A schema library can centralize rules and reuse them at boundaries. These tools do not replace semantic HTML, accessible error relationships, understanding controlled versus uncontrolled inputs, or server-side validation. Select a library when the form's complexity justifies it, and keep the form contract understandable.
A complete React Hook Form example

This shows the core flow: useForm creates helpers, register connects inputs and rules, handleSubmit calls the callback after validation, formState.errors stores field errors, and mode: "onBlur" chooses the timing. The library reduces manual wiring, but does not replace labels, accessible errors, server validation, or handling the request result. Install the package in your own project.

blocks.text: Represent the whole submit lifecycle

A form submission is not finished just because the click handler ran. A typical lifecycle includes idle/edited, client-invalid, submitting, success, and server-error states. Disable duplicate submits when appropriate, show progress feedback, preserve safe entered values after a recoverable error, and never assume a client-side success means a server mutation was authorized or persisted.

blocks.prompt: What makes an input controlled in React?

options.text: React state supplies its value and an onChange handler updates that state
options.feedback: A controlled input displays a value provided by React and reports edits so state can be updated.

options.text: It must be disabled while the component renders
options.feedback: Disabled is an interaction property and does not define controlled versus uncontrolled behavior.

options.text: The browser never keeps an input value
options.feedback: The DOM displays the input value; React state is the source of truth for a controlled input.

options.text: Its value can only be read through FormData on submission
options.feedback: FormData is commonly used for uncontrolled forms; controlled values are available from React state.

blocks.explanation: Controlled input behavior is established by binding value to state and updating state in response to user input.

blocks.prompt: Client-side validation alone is sufficient to enforce security-sensitive data rules.

options.feedback: Client validation can be bypassed; the server must validate and authorize operations independently.
Client-side validation improves experience, while server-side validation is required for trustworthy enforcement.

blocks.explanation: Validation in the UI improves feedback but is not a security boundary.

blocks.prompt: Which practices improve form accessibility and reliability? Select all that apply.

options.text: Associate a field label with its input
options.feedback: A programmatic label helps assistive technology and users identify the purpose of the input.

options.text: Connect field errors to inputs with aria-describedby when appropriate
options.feedback: The relationship can expose the relevant error description when the user focuses the field.

options.text: Use color alone to indicate that a field is invalid
options.feedback: Color alone is not a reliable accessible error indicator; use clear text and semantics too.

options.text: Treat a successful click event as proof that the server saved the form
options.feedback: The client must handle the actual submission result, including server rejection or network failure.

blocks.explanation: Accessible forms make relationships and errors explicit and handle submission as a full asynchronous lifecycle.

options.text: An empty string disables the input
options.feedback: An empty value does not disable the field.

options.text: Changing from undefined to a string can switch the input to controlled

There is no automatic persistence.

options.text: A controlled input cannot be edited
options.feedback: Updating state lets the input change.

blocks.explanation: Initialize controlled text inputs consistently, usually with an empty string.

blocks.prompt: How can SearchForm read an uncontrolled field at submit time?

options.feedback: The browser does not automatically persist it there.
FormData reads named controls from the form.

blocks.prompt: Why use {...current, [name]: value} for a formData object?

options.feedback: That would discard other field values.

value and onChange still define controlled behavior.

items: Controlled inputs are driven by React state; uncontrolled inputs keep their current value in the DOM and can be read at submission.
Native constraints, application rules, and server validation serve complementary roles.
Use labels, associated errors, aria-invalid/aria-describedby where appropriate, and helpful messages.
Model submit lifecycle states explicitly and handle asynchronous failures.
Form libraries reduce wiring; they do not replace semantic HTML, accessibility, or server-side checks.
